analysis.one_liner: Requires electric utilities to get a rising share of their power from renewables and to hit energy-efficiency targets.
analysis.headline: A bill requiring utilities to get 10% rising to 35% of their power from renewables by 2032 was referred to committee and never received a vote or hearing in two years.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required large electric utilities to get at least 10% of their electricity from renewable sources in 2019, rising to 35% by 2032, with the requirement running through 2042. It would also have required large electricity and natural gas utilities to hit steadily rising energy-efficiency targets, so customers would use less energy and pay smaller bills. Utilities could comply by buying tradable renewable credits, paying a fee to states that fund renewable and efficiency programs, or buying verified efficiency savings from other utilities or third parties. The bill never advanced: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy subcommittee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses benefit through lower energy consumption and smaller utility bills, since the efficiency standard requires utilities to cut electricity and gas use (up to 20% cumulative savings for electricity by 2032). People exposed to air pollution from fossil power plants benefit from reduced emissions as renewable generation displaces coal and gas. Renewable energy companies and the energy-efficiency industry (insulation, heat pumps, efficiency contractors) gain a large, guaranteed national market for their products and services.

how_it_helps.text: Requires large electric utilities to obtain a rising share of the electricity they sell from renewable sources — 10% in 2019, climbing to 35% from 2032 through 2042 — creating a guaranteed national market for wind, solar, and other renewable generators.

Requires large electricity and natural gas utilities to meet rising energy-efficiency performance standards, from 1% cumulative electricity savings in 2019 to 20% in 2032, which reduces the total amount of energy customers must pay for.

Allows utilities to buy tradable federal renewable credits or pay alternative compliance fees (with the money routed to state renewable and efficiency programs), designed to find the cheapest renewable power nationwide and hold down compliance costs.
Clarifies that states may set rates for voluntary renewable production incentive programs, preserving state authority over clean-energy policy.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel generators and the utilities that depend on them would lose market share as renewables take a growing slice of electricity sales, and utilities would bear the cost of compliance, efficiency programs, and renewable credit purchases. Some of those compliance costs would likely be passed on to customers through rates, though the efficiency savings themselves reduce bills.

drawbacks.text: The renewable standard is a mandate on utilities, and its compliance costs would be recovered through rates, so some of the cost would land on consumers' electric bills, particularly in regions with fewer renewable resources.

Utilities could avoid the renewable standard by paying an alternative compliance fee of $50 per megawatt-hour rather than actually building renewable generation, which weakens the guarantee that new renewable capacity gets built.

The bill allows utilities to meet the efficiency standard by purchasing savings from third-party providers rather than delivering efficiency to their own customers, which could concentrate the benefits in compliance paperwork rather than household upgrades.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pursued large, real public benefits—slower growth in electric and gas bills, reduced air pollution, and a durable renewables market—at a cost borne mainly by fossil-fuel generators and, to a lesser extent, utility customers through compliance spending. Its design included genuine safeguards for cost (compliance-payment caps tied to inflation, state flexibility, cost-effectiveness tests, a NAS review), so the objection that it would raise rates has to be weighed against the requirement that utilities pursue only cost-effective efficiency. The chief weakness is its reliance on a compliance market whose costs depend on FERC and DOE implementation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which referred it to its Energy Subcommittee, and it sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote for the rest of the two-year Congress.

narrative.text: H.R. 2746 was introduced by Rep. Peter Welch on May 25, 2017 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On June 9, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy — the last action of any kind in the bill's record.
The bill attracted 10 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further committee or floor action ever occurred before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The fossil-fuel power sector and utilities that did not want a federal renewable or efficiency mandate are better off; the standard never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel power generators and utilities

industries.industry: Renewable energy generators (wind, solar, geothermal, biomass, hydropower)
industries.note: The bill creates a guaranteed national demand for renewable electricity through a federal standard and a tradable credit market, plus bonus credits for small-scale, tribal-land, and brownfield projects. Every megawatt-hour of renewable generation becomes more valuable.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel power generators (coal, oil, and conventional natural gas)
industries.note: A federal renewable standard directly displaces the share of the electricity market these generators supply, and the efficiency standard shrinks total demand for their fuel and power.

Utilities bear new federal compliance obligations and reporting costs, but the bill encourages state regulators to let them recover their efficiency-program costs and even earn shareholder incentives for meeting the standards, so the burden is partly softened.

industries.industry: Energy efficiency and weatherization industry (contractors, ESCOs, third-party efficiency providers)
industries.note: The efficiency standard creates a large, steady market for building upgrades, combined heat and power, and efficiency services, which utilities may buy from third-party providers to meet their targets.
Gas utilities above a size threshold face their own efficiency performance standard, requiring them to reduce customer gas consumption — a direct hit to a business model built on selling more fuel.
